title: Weighing Down the Future: Long-Term Effects of Childhood Obesity on Intergenerational Mobility
author: Fan, Maoyong; Jin, Yanhong; Zhang, Man
summary: A major study finds children obese in adolescence end up approximately twenty percentile points lower on the adult income ladder than normal-weight peers, with effects compounding through education, occupation, and persistent health problems. The impact falls heaviest on girls and lower-income families. The research cuts against modern inclinations to separate physical formation from moral and economic formation, revealing how bodily care constitutes a form of cultural inheritance that shapes life trajectories across domains.
points: Childhood obesity predicts adult income approximately 20 percentile points lower than normal-weight peers—substantial intergenerational mobility effects.
Physical formation consequences compound through education, occupational sorting, and persistent health challenges across adult life.
Impact falls hardest on girls and children from lower-income families, creating stratified life outcomes based on childhood body status.
How a child's body is fed, moved, trained, and cared for constitutes one of the most consequential forms of cultural inheritance.
Physical formation is never merely private; the body carries consequences of cultural inattention into every domain of adult flourishing.
